rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. Midrange temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.
Change only gradient duration to test whether the early coeluting cluster separates with a shallower slope. This also reveals whether resolution gains justify the added retention time.

Probe temperature selectivity at the faster scouting slope, since slope reduction alone did not resolve the early cluster. Higher temperature may separate those compounds while keeping the last peak within 10 minutes.

Retain the favorable high-temperature selectivity and use a shallower gradient to improve the remaining critical pair. The last peak should still elute before 10 minutes, leaving room to reach the maximum score.

The remaining critical pair worsened with a shallower gradient, so test a higher starting organic fraction to shift selectivity rather than simply extending the gradient. Keep the favorable temperature and check that the early peaks remain adequately retained and separated.
Injection 5 reached the maximum CRF; shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Monitor the early cluster, whose resolution margins are smallest.

Slightly narrow the gradient window to recover resolution in both marginal early pairs while retaining the shorter gradient duration. This slope lies between injections 5 and 6 and should keep the last peak within the gradient.

Test whether a one-step increase in starting organic fraction can shorten retention while preserving full resolution. Injection 7 remains the fastest maximum-score method; watch for compression of the early cluster and insufficient retention of the first peak.

Test temperature selectivity one step below 60 C while holding the fastest fully resolved gradient fixed. This will show whether a modest temperature reduction improves the critical-pair margins enough to permit further gradient acceleration.

Return to 60 C and test a gradient slope between the fully resolved injection 7 and the slightly underresolved injection 6. The narrower endpoint should still encompass the last peak’s elution composition, potentially giving a faster maximum-score method.

Probe the opposite temperature limit for a different elution order and potentially better critical-pair selectivity, retaining injection 7 as the fully resolved benchmark. Injection 10 is slightly underresolved despite its rounded CRF of 1.000.

Reduce the endpoint one step from injection 10 to recover the small resolution deficit while keeping a six-minute gradient. The last peak should elute near the gradient end, with substantially less hold risk than a more aggressive endpoint reduction.

Test whether a shallower gradient can recover the early-pair resolution lost at the higher starting fraction in injection 8. This explores a second fully resolved operating window while keeping the last peak comfortably below 10 minutes.

Return to the successful starting fraction and test a shallower slope for a larger minimum-resolution margin. The last peak is expected before 10 minutes, so this may provide a more robust maximum-score alternative to injection 7.

Use a shallower slope at the higher starting fraction to push the remaining critical pair above 1.5. This tests whether the alternative window can achieve full resolution; injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Lower the endpoint one grid step from injection 15 to resolve its marginal early pair. This should establish a fully resolved alternative starting window while keeping the last peak below the time-penalty threshold.

Test the unexamined starting fraction between 0.05 and 0.15 at the same slope as injection 7 to isolate its selectivity effect. If it improves the limiting pair, it may permit a steeper, faster fully resolved gradient.

Refine around injection 7 by lowering the endpoint one step, seeking a little more critical-pair clearance for a modest retention-time increase. The tested alternatives have not beaten its combination of full resolution and speed.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 14 to increase the limiting-pair resolution margin while targeting last elution before 10 minutes. Injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; this run seeks a more robust maximum-score alternative.

Test the remaining endpoint between injections 7 and 6 to pinpoint the fastest fully resolved eight-minute gradient. This is a boundary check: the critical pair may fall just below 1.5, in which case injection 7 remains preferred.

The faster boundary tests lost resolution, so back off to a shallower, untested eight-minute gradient to strengthen critical-pair separation while retaining maximum CRF. Injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Refine the fully resolved region with a slightly shallower eight-minute gradient, targeting improved critical-pair clearance without a time penalty. Retain injection 7 as the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test a six-minute gradient with the same slope as fully resolved injection 21 but a lower endpoint. The early separations should be preserved; this checks whether the final hold still clears the last compound before 10 minutes.

Use an intermediate slope between injections 22 and 14 to retain full resolution with additional critical-pair margin and no expected time penalty. Injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method; this run refines a more conservative maximum-score alternative.

Use the final injection on an untested method with the same successful slope as injection 21, predicting full resolution and last elution near 6.7 minutes. Injection 7 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method and the preferred campaign result.
